summary:
Stephen Chin, leading Developer Relations at Neo4j, presents on Agentic GraphRAG while noting his ongoing O'Reilly book on the topic. He frames the core problem: agentic systems suffer from hallucinations and biases, as demonstrated by an OpenAI reasoning API example where the model showed gender bias and incorrect mathematical reasoning when asked about fitting girls in a classroom grid. LLMs excel at language tasks but lack genuine reasoning, creating gaps that knowledge graphs can fill.

He describes agentic systems where agents observe, think, and act through an orchestration layer with GenAI models and tools. Monolithic architectures are hard to maintain, secure, or modify. MCP (Model Context Protocol) addresses this by separating tools and data sources into a client-server model. Neo4j built MCP tools including a Cypher query generator, a memory module, and cloud API provisioning.

Agent memory providers like Zep, Cognney, and Memz run on Neo4j as their core graph database. A video search and summarization architecture demonstrates combining graph RAG and vector pipelines. GraphRAG offers advantages over direct LLMs (generic responses) and baseline RAG (incomplete due to vector similarity not equaling relevance). The recommended pattern performs vector search first, maps embeddings to graph nodes, then pulls back related nodes and context using cosine similarity or community grouping algorithms. Neo4j creates node structures from unstructured data using LLMs and attaches text embeddings as node properties. Framework integrations include LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and experimental LangGraph prototypes for agents.

A customer case study shows an enterprise replacing SaaS systems with GraphRAG, achieving 250,000 employee questions in year one, 2,000 daily queries, and 85% adoption. In Q&A, Chin defers MCP memory server implementation details to Michael Hunger's session and notes LangGraph is the agent framework from the LangChain team, recommending users pick whichever tool works best since Neo4j integrates with all. Resources mentioned include Neo4j's Certified Developer program and the annual Nodes conference.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Stephen Chin introduces himself as head of Developer Relations at Neo4j, mentions his upcoming O'Reilly book on GraphRAG, and polls the audience on familiarity with graph databases and GraphRAG.

sections.title: Problem with LLM Reasoning and Biases
sections.summary: Demonstrates how OpenAI reasoning API exhibits bias and incorrect reasoning on a classroom grid problem, showing LLMs lack genuine reasoning despite appearing intelligent. Notes the danger in domains like drug discovery and supply chain.

sections.title: Agentic Architecture and MCP Solution
sections.summary: Describes agentic systems where agents observe, think, and act. Explains limitations of monolithic architectures and introduces MCP as a solution. Neo4j built MCP tools including Cypher query generation, memory module, and cloud APIs.

sections.title: Agent Memory and Graph-Based Systems
sections.summary: Covers agent memory providers (Zep, Cognney, Memz) running on Neo4j. Shows a video search and summarization architecture with both graph RAG and vector pipelines, highlighting GraphRAG's lower hallucination rates.

sections.title: GraphRAG Patterns and Architecture
sections.summary: Compares direct LLMs, baseline RAG, and GraphRAG. Explains the recommended pattern: vector search first, then map embeddings to graph nodes and pull back related context. Covers text-to-Cypher, pre/post filtering, and context window behavior. References Microsoft GraphRAG paper.

sections.title: Customer Example and Resources
sections.summary: Shares CLA customer case with 250k questions, 2,000 daily queries, 85% adoption. Promotes Neo4j Certified Developer program and Nodes conference. Q&A clarifies the vector-search-then-graph-traversal pattern.

sections.title: Q&A: Embeddings, Framework Integrations, and LangChain vs LangGraph
sections.summary: Stephen explains how embeddings point to graph nodes and cosine similarity or community grouping algorithms identify relevant context. In simple architectures, embedded chunks and nodes are the same; Neo4j uses LLMs to create node structures from unstructured data and attaches text embeddings as node properties. Neo4j integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and has experimental LangGraph prototypes. He defers MCP memory server details to Michael Hunger's session. On LangChain vs LangGraph, he notes LangGraph is the agent framework from LangChain creators and recommends using whichever tool works best, as Neo4j integrates with all.
